references.text: The same expression about being 'cut off from one's people' is used for the one who eats blood, showing that this is a fixed penalty for serious violations of God's law.
Earlier in the same chapter, there is a warning against doing any of these 'abominable things' (תּוֹעֵבוֹת), which shows the context for the punishment mentioned in verse 29.
A parallel legal text describing the same penalty—being cut off from the people—for sexual sins listed in chapter 18.
The expression 'be cut off from Israel' (וְנִכְרְתָה) is used for the one who eats leavened bread during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, showing consistent use of this penalty.
The same penalty—being cut off from the people—applies to the one who profanes the Sabbath.
The first time the expression 'be cut off from one's people' is used in the Torah, regarding the uncircumcised man who breaks the covenant.
Explains that the one who sins with a high hand (willfully) shall be cut off from the people because he has despised the Lord's word.
Uses the same word for 'abominable' (תּוֹעֵבָה) regarding the practices of the Canaanites, which is the reason they were driven out of the land.
